name: Fundamentals of Testing
summary: Understand what testing achieves, why defects occur, and how testers collaborate throughout the test process.

topics.title: Testing, verification and validation
topics.body: Testing evaluates software work products and helps reveal defects and risks. Verification checks whether specified requirements are fulfilled. Validation checks whether the software meets user needs in its operational context.
topics.example: An online banking page may satisfy its written password specification but still be difficult for customers to use. Verification and validation ask different questions.

topics.title: Errors, defects and failures
topics.body: A human error can introduce a defect into a document or code. When the defect is executed under relevant conditions it may cause an observable failure. A root cause explains why the error occurred.
topics.example: An engineer misunderstands the upper age boundary (error), writes '< 60' instead of '<= 60' (defect), and a 60-year-old customer is rejected (failure).

topics.title: Seven testing principles
topics.body: Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects. Exhaustive testing is impossible. Early testing saves time and money. Defects cluster together. Tests wear out. Testing is context dependent. The absence-of-defects fallacy warns that a defect-free product may still be unfit for users.
topics.example: Repeatedly running the same passing regression tests can miss new risks; refresh test ideas as the product evolves.

topics.title: Test activities and traceability
topics.body: The test process includes planning, monitoring and control, analysis, design, implementation, execution, and completion. Traceability connects the test basis, tests and results, supporting coverage measurement and impact analysis.
topics.example: Link each acceptance criterion to its test cases and results so you can see what would be affected by a requirement change.

topics.title: Skills, teamwork and independence
topics.body: Testing requires analytical thinking, careful communication and domain knowledge. Whole-team collaboration helps share quality responsibility. Independent perspectives can spot different defects, but excessive separation can damage collaboration.
topics.example: A QA engineer questions an assumption that developers and business analysts have accepted without noticing the risk.

name: Testing Throughout the SDLC
summary: Learn how testing works in different development models and at different levels.

topics.title: Testing in every SDLC
topics.body: Testing is relevant to every software development activity, whether the team uses a sequential, iterative or incremental model. Test-first approaches use tests or acceptance criteria to guide development.
topics.example: For a login story, derive acceptance tests when the team clarifies its expected behavior rather than waiting for the completed screen.

topics.title: Shift-left, DevOps and retrospectives
topics.body: Shift-left moves suitable quality activities earlier in development. DevOps encourages collaboration, automation and frequent reliable delivery. Retrospectives help teams learn from their working practices.
topics.example: Review a proposed API contract before coding and run automated regression tests on every integration build.

topics.title: Test levels
topics.body: Common levels are component, component integration, system, system integration and acceptance testing. Each has a distinct objective and typical test basis.
topics.example: Test a password validation function alone, then authentication service integration, then the complete customer login flow.

topics.title: Test types, confirmation and regression
topics.body: Functional testing concerns what a system does; non-functional testing evaluates how well it behaves. Confirmation testing checks a fix; regression testing looks for unwanted effects in unchanged parts after changes.
topics.example: After a timeout defect is fixed, recheck that timeout and also rerun neighboring authentication flows.

topics.title: Maintenance testing
topics.body: Changes, migration and retirement can trigger maintenance testing. The scope depends on change impact and risk.
topics.example: Migrating existing customer records to a new database requires checks for data correctness and compatibility.

name: Static Testing
summary: Identify defects without executing the software, through reviews and static analysis.

topics.title: Static vs dynamic testing
topics.body: Static testing examines work products without executing software. Reviews apply to requirements, stories, designs, code and test documents. Static analysis can find certain code issues. Dynamic testing exercises running software.
topics.example: Spot a contradictory requirement in a document before any code is written.

topics.title: Why early feedback matters
topics.body: Feedback shared early and frequently can prevent misunderstandings from spreading into design, implementation and tests.
topics.example: A business analyst clarifies a missing password-reset acceptance criterion during story review.

topics.title: Review process
topics.body: The review process includes planning, review initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, and fixing and reporting. Roles may include author, manager, facilitator, scribe and review leader.
topics.example: A scribe records anomalies while the facilitator keeps a review meeting productive.

topics.title: Review types
topics.body: Informal reviews, walkthroughs, technical reviews and inspections differ in objectives, formality, roles and documentation. Pick the approach suited to the context.
topics.example: A walkthrough can help the author explain a design, while an inspection follows a more formal defect-detection process.

name: Test Analysis and Design
summary: Choose and apply black-box, white-box and experience-based testing techniques.

topics.title: Equivalence partitioning
topics.body: Partition input or output data into groups expected to be handled in the same way, then test representative values. Consider both valid and invalid partitions.
topics.example: If valid ages are 18 to 60, choose values from below 18, inside 18–60, and above 60.

topics.title: Boundary value analysis
topics.body: Test at the boundaries between partitions, where faults commonly occur. Two-value and three-value BVA choose different numbers of values around each boundary.
topics.example: For the age range 18–60, two-value boundary checks include 17, 18, 60 and 61.

topics.title: Decision tables
topics.body: Use conditions, resulting actions and rules to design tests for combinations of business decisions. Check for missing, contradictory or impossible rules.
topics.example: Discount eligibility might depend on membership and whether a return deadline was missed.

topics.title: State transitions
topics.body: Model system states, events and valid transitions. Tests can cover states or transitions and expose inappropriate behavior across sequences.
topics.example: A locked account should not go directly from Locked to Authenticated without satisfying the unlock rule.

topics.title: White-box coverage
topics.body: Statement testing measures which executable statements were run. Branch testing measures which branches were exercised. A high coverage percentage is not proof that all faults were detected.
topics.example: Tests may run every statement while still missing an important conditional branch.

topics.title: Experience-based and collaborative techniques
topics.body: Error guessing, exploratory and checklist-based testing use knowledge and experience. Collaborative story writing and ATDD link acceptance criteria to shared examples and tests.
topics.example: Use past production incidents to shape exploratory login testing, then agree on acceptance examples with the whole team.

name: Managing Test Activities
summary: Plan, prioritize, monitor and report testing using risk and reliable evidence.

topics.title: Test plans and criteria
topics.body: A test plan describes objectives, scope, approach, resources and schedule. Entry and exit criteria help decide when activities can start or finish.
topics.example: A release might require all critical tests passed and no unresolved severe defects before signing off.

topics.title: Estimation and prioritization
topics.body: Estimate effort using experience, ratios or other structured techniques. Prioritize tests based on risk, coverage and business importance. The test pyramid emphasizes many focused low-level tests.
topics.example: Test payment authorization before an infrequently used visual preference when release time is limited.

topics.title: Risk management
topics.body: Product risk combines likelihood with impact; project risks threaten delivery rather than the product itself. Test thoroughness should reflect risk, and risk control may reduce or mitigate risk.
topics.example: A potential money-transfer defect is high impact and deserves strong test coverage even if it is not common.

topics.title: Monitoring and test reports
topics.body: Track progress using meaningful metrics and communicate coverage, defect trends, remaining risk and exit-criteria status. Reports should be adapted to their audience.
topics.example: A release manager needs a clear readiness summary, while developers need precise failing-test evidence.

topics.title: Configuration and defects
topics.body: Configuration management keeps work products and versions identifiable. Defect reports describe reproducible steps, expected/actual results, impact and supporting evidence.
topics.example: Report a login defect with environment, build, test data, timestamps and screenshots to help reproduce it.

name: Test Tools
summary: Understand tool support and the benefits and risks of automation.

topics.title: Tool support for testing
topics.body: Tools support management, static testing, test design, execution, measurement and collaboration. Their value depends on appropriate selection and use.
topics.example: Use Playwright for repeatable web regression checks and a test-management tool to report coverage.

topics.title: Automation benefits and risks
topics.body: Automation can improve repeatability, save effort and speed feedback, but can bring maintenance costs, false confidence, technical problems and unrealistic expectations.
topics.example: An unstable UI selector can make a test fail even when the product works; maintain reliable checks and review results.
